stem: An attacker writes code into the address space of a running, trusted process and causes that process to execute it, so the activity appears to come from a legitimate application. Which vulnerability type is being exploited?

options.text: Memory injection
options.why: Writing into another process's memory and executing from there is the defining behaviour. It is attractive because the malicious code inherits the host process's trust and often its privileges.

options.text: An operating system based vulnerability
options.why: The OS may provide the mechanism abused, and the weakness being exploited sits in the application process.

options.text: A firmware vulnerability
options.why: Firmware sits beneath the operating system, in the device itself.

options.text: A cloud-specific vulnerability
options.why: Cloud-specific issues are overwhelmingly configuration and identity, not in-process memory manipulation.

stem: A flaw lets an attacker persist beneath the operating system, surviving a full reinstall and remaining invisible to endpoint protection. Where does this vulnerability sit?

options.text: Firmware
options.why: Firmware loads before the OS, so it survives reinstallation and sits below anything the OS can inspect. That persistence and invisibility is exactly why firmware flaws matter disproportionately.

options.text: The operating system
options.why: An OS flaw would not survive wiping and reinstalling the OS.

options.text: The application layer
options.why: Applications sit above the OS and are removed with it.

options.text: A supply chain compromise of the software provider
options.why: Possible as the delivery route, and the question asks where the weakness resides.

stem: A cloud storage bucket holding customer exports is readable by anyone on the internet. The provider's platform is fully patched. What kind of vulnerability is this, and what fixes it?

options.text: Cloud-specific, arising from configuration and identity rather than software, and fixed by correcting the resource policy
options.why: The overwhelming majority of cloud incidents are customer misconfiguration. There is no patch to apply because nothing is unpatched.

options.text: An operating system vulnerability in the storage service, fixed by patching
options.why: The provider maintains the service and the stem says it is current. Reaching for patching here is the instinct this topic exists to correct.

options.text: A firmware vulnerability in the provider's hardware
options.why: Nothing about the scenario involves device firmware, and it would be the provider's responsibility regardless.

options.text: A zero-day, since no patch is available
options.why: A zero-day is an unknown flaw with no patch yet. A permission you set incorrectly is neither unknown nor awaiting a fix.

stem: Network appliances are found to contain an undocumented administrative account, present from manufacture and not introduced by anyone in the buying organisation. Which vulnerability type is this?

options.text: A hardware provider supply chain vulnerability
options.why: The weakness arrived with the product. No action by the purchaser introduced it, and no action after delivery would have prevented it, which is why the control is procurement, vendor assessment and verification.

options.text: A misconfiguration by the purchasing organisation
options.why: The stem rules this out explicitly: the account was there from manufacture.

options.text: An end-of-life vulnerability
options.why: End of life means support has ceased. Nothing here says the product is unsupported.

options.text: A cloud-specific vulnerability
options.why: These are physical appliances in the purchaser's estate.

stem: A critical flaw is published for a product whose vendor ceased support two years ago. How should this be classified and handled?

options.text: An end-of-life vulnerability: no patch will ever exist, so the response is compensating controls or replacement
options.why: End of life is called out separately because it removes the usual remedy. Isolation, access restriction and monitoring carry the system until it is replaced.

options.text: A zero-day, because no patch is available
options.why: A zero-day is unknown to the vendor with no patch yet available. Here the vendor is known and simply no longer producing patches.

options.text: An unpatched vulnerability, remediated by applying the latest update
options.why: There is no latest update. That is the whole difficulty.

options.text: A configuration vulnerability, remediated by hardening alone
options.why: Hardening reduces exposure and does not remove the flaw in the code, which is why isolation and a replacement plan are needed too.

stem: A vendor publishes a kernel update fixing a local privilege escalation flaw affecting all supported versions. Which vulnerability category does this fall into?

options.text: Operating system based
options.why: The kernel is the operating system. The fix comes from the OS vendor and is applied through normal patch management.

options.text: Firmware
options.why: Firmware sits below the OS in the device and is updated separately, usually far less often.

options.text: Application based
options.why: Applications run above the OS. A kernel flaw affects everything on the host.

options.text: Supply chain
options.why: A flaw written by the vendor in its own code is an ordinary defect, not a supply chain compromise.

stem: Which TWO vulnerability types cannot be resolved by applying a vendor patch? (Choose two.)

options.text: End-of-life products, where the vendor no longer issues updates
options.why: No patch is coming, so the response is compensating controls and replacement planning.

options.text: Cloud misconfiguration, such as an over-permissive resource policy
options.why: Nothing is unpatched. The fix is configuration, which is why patching is the wrong instinct in cloud.

options.text: An operating system kernel flaw
options.why: Resolved by the OS vendor's patch.

options.text: A buffer overflow in a vendor application
options.why: Fixed in code and delivered as an update.

options.text: A firmware flaw in a current, supported device
options.why: Firmware updates are rarer and riskier to apply, and for a supported device one does exist.
